EPA / CDC list pregnancy and early childhood as sensitive periods for arsenic exposure.
EPA Lead and Copper Rule action level 0.015 mg/L (15 ppb); MCLG is zero (no known safe level). EPA's 2024 Lead and Copper Rule Improvements lower the action level to 10 ppb (compliance ~2027).
EPA / CDC: infants, children and pregnancy are most at risk from lead.
EPA MCL 10 mg/L as nitrogen (40 CFR 141.62). NC 02L standard is also 10 mg/L.
EPA / CDC: infants under 6 months are most at risk (methemoglobinemia); pregnancy also listed by CDC.
USGS / NC DEQ: fertilizer application and recharge from rain can raise shallow-groundwater nitrate in spring.
EPA MCL 1 mg/L as nitrogen (40 CFR 141.62).
same sensitive groups as nitrate (EPA / CDC).
EPA MCL 30 µg/L (ppb), Radionuclides Rule (40 CFR 141.66).
EPA secondary standard (SMCL) 0.05 mg/L (50 ppb), aesthetic. NC 02L groundwater standard is also 50 µg/L.
EPA lifetime health advisory 0.3 mg/L (300 ppb); EPA advises applying it to infants under 6 months.
EPA secondary standard (SMCL) 0.3 mg/L (300 ppb), aesthetic only.
EPA Lead and Copper Rule action level 1.3 mg/L (MCLG 1.3 mg/L). EPA SMCL is 1.0 mg/L (taste/staining).
EPA lists infants and people with Wilson's disease as more sensitive to copper.
EPA MCL 4.0 mg/L (bone effects); EPA SMCL 2.0 mg/L (dental fluorosis in children).
EPA: children under 9 are at risk of dental fluorosis above 2 mg/L.
EPA Revised Total Coliform Rule: presence triggers corrective action; private wells should test absent.
CDC: infants, older adults and people with weakened immune systems are most at risk from waterborne germs.
EPA MCL for E. coli: any confirmed presence is a violation (40 CFR 141.63).
EPA secondary standard 6.5–8.5, aesthetic.
no EPA or NC limit. Bands from USGS water-hardness classification (mg/L as CaCO₃).
USGS: 0–60 soft, 61–120 moderately hard, 121–180 hard, >180 very hard.
there is NO final federal limit. EPA's 1999 proposal: MCL 300 pCi/L, or an alternative MCL of 4,000 pCi/L where a state runs an indoor-air radon program. NC has no private-well radon standard.
EPA PFAS National Primary Drinking Water Regulation (April 2024): PFOA MCL 4.0 ppt (ng/L). In 2025 EPA said it would keep the PFOA/PFOS MCLs but extend compliance to 2031.
EPA 2024 PFAS rule: PFOS MCL 4.0 ppt.
EPA 2024 PFAS rule: HFPO-DA (GenX) MCL 10 ppt. In 2025 EPA announced it intends to rescind and reconsider this limit; NC DEQ PFAS programs may use a different threshold.
EPA lists pregnancy, infants and children as sensitive to PFAS exposure.

manufacturer / extension service guidance for greensand and softeners.

EPA fluoride MCL 4.0 mg/L (skeletal fluorosis) and SMCL 2.0 mg/L (dental fluorosis).
CDC: diarrhea, cramps, nausea, vomiting from waterborne pathogens.
NC DHHS shock chlorination guidance.
EPA / NSF/ANSI 55 Class A UV systems.
NC groundwater, especially Piedmont/mountain wells, is often slightly acidic (USGS / NC DEQ).
USGS: harder groundwater is more common in limestone areas of the NC Coastal Plain.

NC DEQ: PFAS including GenX from the Chemours Fayetteville Works plant has been found in private wells in the lower Cape Fear area; PFAS also come from firefighting foam, landfills and some biosolids.
EPA PFAS rule health basis: some cancers, liver, immune and developmental effects, and cholesterol changes.
EPA / NSF: RO (NSF/ANSI 58) and certified carbon (NSF/ANSI 53) filters reduce PFOA/PFOS.
EPA radon: main risk is lung cancer from inhaling radon released from water; small stomach-cancer risk from drinking.
EPA: aeration removes up to ~99%; GAC is effective but the filter can become radioactive.

facts are reused from LearnContent / ContaminantInfo, which carry their own VERIFY notes. / Alternates "where it comes from" and "who is most at risk" from the Learn article, falling back / to the contaminant's summary. Short: at most two sentences.
"usually highest" comes from the county forecast. The bundled county_trends.csv is placeholder sample data, so the card shows a "Sample data" label until real aggregates replace it.
CDC / NC DHHS guidance after a positive E. coli test: use bottled (or boiled) water for drinking, cooking and brushing teeth until the well is disinfected and retested.
NC began requiring testing of newly constructed private wells in July 2008 (NC DHHS / 15A NCAC 18A).
